title: Degeneracy Cannot Violate the Quantum Hamming Bound
abstract: The quantum Hamming bound is the standard finite-length sphere-packing bound for exact correction of arbitrary qubit errors. Whether degeneracy can evade this bound has remained unresolved in full generality for nearly three decades: distinct correctable errors may act identically on the code space, so the usual disjoint-sphere argument breaks down. We prove that every exact binary quantum subspace code with $K>1$ obeys the bound, without assuming either nondegeneracy or additivity. Our proof turns the Li--Xing linear-programming polynomial into an exact intersection count for quaternary Hamming balls. Monotonicity in block length and in ball-center separation then reduces the problem to a local node--edge charging inequality at the shortest admissible length. Thus degeneracy can merge correctable error sectors, but cannot enlarge the finite-length binary Hamming bound.
summary: This paper resolves a decades-old question in quantum coding theory: whether code degeneracy can violate the Quantum Hamming Bound. The authors prove that despite complex error overlaps allowed by degeneracy, the bound remains inviolable for all exact binary quantum subspace codes. They achieve this using sophisticated combinatorial methods involving transforming linear programming bounds into local node-edge charging inequalities.
main_problem: To rigorously prove that quantum error-correcting codes, even those exhibiting degeneracy (where distinct errors act identically), cannot violate the fundamental Quantum Hamming Bound.
main_result: The authors prove that every exact binary quantum subspace code with more than one logical qubit ($K>1$) must satisfy the established Quantum Hamming Bound. Degeneracy allows error sectors to overlap but does not permit an enlargement of this finite-length bound.
method: The proof combines advanced combinatorial techniques, transforming a linear programming problem into an exact intersection count for quaternary Hamming balls. This is reduced via monotonicity arguments to analyzing local node-edge charging inequalities at the shortest admissible code length.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on abstract mathematical structures: exact binary quantum subspace codes $((n, K, d))$ designed to correct Pauli errors up to a certain weight $t$. The underlying mathematics involves Fourier transforms and counting vectors in Hamming spaces over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
key_observables: The normalized collision ratio $R_{n,t}(s)$, which must be less than or equal to 1 for the bound to hold. Other key observables include collision multiplicities ($C_s, I_s$) and related ratios ($u_s$).
important_parameters: Block length $n$, code dimension factor $K$, error correction radius $t = \lfloor(d-1)/2floor$, and the support size $s$ used in local analysis.
main_assumptions: The proof assumes the existence of an exact binary quantum subspace code structure. The final steps rely on complex combinatorial identities derived from orthogonal polynomials (Krawtchouk polynomials) to establish positivity and inequality chains.
figures_summary: Not specified, but the notes detail the derivation of recurrence relations for collision multiplicities ($C_{s+1} = C_s - I_s$) and the establishment of bounds using polynomial inequalities.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the connection to linear programming bounds (Li-Xing). It then uses Fourier reduction to map the problem onto additive Hamming space structures. The core is a multi-stage combinatorial proof: reducing the global bound to local node-edge charging inequalities, and finally deriving explicit polynomial certificates that confirm these local constraints are satisfied.
why_interesting: This work provides deep mathematical insight into the fundamental limits of quantum error correction codes, which underpins all practical quantum computing architectures. It settles a long-standing open problem by providing rigorous combinatorial proofs applicable to general subspace codes, not just stabilizer codes.
